191789:
LD 1793 - Testimony of Ed Meadows IN FAVOR
April 28, 2025
SenatorTepler, Representative Doudera and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Environment and Natural Resources:
I am Ed Meadows, resident of Trenton, near Ellsworth. I am representing myself (and not any interest group).
Thank you for the opportunity to speak in favor of this bill.
The bill has many benefits and no downsides.
In many Maine towns, like Trenton, the cost of solid waste disposal is the second highest line item in the town budget - only after the cost of education. It`s a direct increase in
local property tax.
I've lived in six different towns in Maine and three other states. Thus, I've seen many
different ways towns and states deal with solid waste.
I was appointed to the Trenton Solid Waste Committee to help work on this issue. We
have focused on costs, in effort to contain property tax burden. (These comments are mine and do not reflect the Town of Trenton, or the Solid Waste Committee.)
In Maine there is no coordinated system for waste disposal. Each town deals with it as
best they can. Some towns have town-wide pick up. Others don't. About one-third of Maine towns use the "pay to throw" system. But not others. In other states solid
waste is handled by the county or regional entity to take advantage of economies of scale.
Recycling costs more per ton than solid waste disposal. lt's cheaper to just throw everything in the trash. That just adds to the problem of running out of landfill space.
Many people are unaware of how the costs work. Let's say you pay someone to pick up
your trash. That is not the end of the story. The truck takes it to transfer station, landfill, or wherever it goes. The town is then billed for the tonnage. That cost goes into the town budget, to be added to your property tax. So you pay twice.
How your town does it may not be how the next town over handles it.
I recall when the State created the Maine Waste Management Agency. It had many of the goals in LD 1793. But the agency was eliminated in state budget cuts and government
downsizing thirty years ago. Since then, the problem has only intensified.
Trying to deal with this locally feels like it is "every town for itself." We need a better way

LD 1793 - In favor. Ed Meadows, Page 2, April 28, 2025
Many towns in eastern Maine are trying to work with the disposal facilities in Hampden
and Orrington. However, constant delays, equipment problems and financial setbacks
make it difficult for any certainty about when they may operate. These facilities do present the opportunity to rethink how waste is collected, transported and handled.
Let's say a town wants to explore a more cost effective method of collection and disposal. ~ Where do they get the data to make a cost analysis? - Where can they find models of places that have done this successfully?
That is what LD 1793 is all about.
The bill authorizes the DEP to provide leadership to resolve these problems. I saw how important this is when I served as Commissioner of the Department of Conservation.
Legislative support gives weight to the department's role in convening stakeholders.
This support directs everyone to think of better ways of collection and handling, with emphasis on efficiency and cost reduction - to the state, towns, businesses and taxpayers.
The bill provides what towns need:
� A central source of information
Q Technical assistance
0 Possible grant funds to implement solutions
I A task force of knowledgeable people to examine the issue and identify solutions
I It requests a report back with options for solutions.
Personally, I'd rather see more immediate action right now.
But, my experience with complex public policy issues says the idea of carefully
evaluating long-term solutions can be a good first step.
Finally, fill. Yes, there may be cost with this. However, based on what we see all over
the state, the cost of the program in this LD is likely far less than being spent now, town by town. Doing these things likely involves less time and less cost than the cost and time now directed by state and local governments, and private business to these issues.
Or, the costs to everybody will be lower over time.
This LD addresses critical issues. it points us in a better direction for the future.
l urge you to support passage of this much-needed LD. Thank you.
Ed Meadows, Trenton; avocet201 4@yahoo.com; cell 517-974-3064

10051446:
Revised
Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association In Opposition to
LD 1793, An Act to Improve Management and Reduce the Volume of Solid Waste
May 5, 2025 ________________________________________________________________
Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Environment and Natural Resources, my name is Kate Dufour, and I am submitting revised testimony on LD 1793 because our Legislative Policy Committee decided to oppose the initiative at its April 29 meeting.
As expected, access to technical and financial assistance and collaborating on how best to support the local level solid waste management responsibilities provided in the bill are appreciated. However, considering that human nature and behavior impact municipalities' ability to respond to recycling goals and hierarchy, there is concern that the development and implementation of rules, policies, programs, and incentives designed to reduce the volume of solid waste will increase the workloads on municipal employees and costs to provide related services, without any change in outcome.
However, Sen. Grohoski has reached out to see if issues could be resolved. While we have not had the opportunity to meet, MMA and its members are willing to discuss other options, especially those focused on public education. To the extent that time allows, there may be a middle ground to be found.
Thank you for your consideration of the municipal perspective on this issue.

10046991:
Good Day Members of the Environment and Natural Resources Committee,
The Winterport Solid Waste and Recycling Committee wishes to testify in support of LD 1793 and in particular the funding for grants under the Maine Solid Waste Diversion Grant Program. Winterport is a small community of about 4000 residents. We were interested in developing a food waste diversion pilot project in our community. We projected we could remove 13 tons of food waste from our MSW thereby keeping it out of the Juniper Ridge landfill. The cost of collection and transport to a composting facility was the largest cost associated with the project and those costs are prohibited by the grant. Once we ascertained that, we abandoned the effort.
Recycling may also end up in our MSW because there are no facilities in mid-Maine that will take our recyclable material. Our costs to transport to ecomaine in southern Maine are double what transport with tipping fees to Juniper Ridge would cost the town. The pilot program established in this bill would go a long way towards identifying reasonable solutions for small municipalities in our region.
The DEP rules themselves discourage small communities from developing any solid waste diversion programs. And discourage development of facilities that might be able to accommodate waste streams that the Department has prioritized. Any barriers to diverting material that can be removed from landfill waste need to be removed.
Action on these issues is long overdue. This bill will move us forward. It is our hope that you will unanimously vote it out of Committee as Ought To Pass.
Respectfully, Alan Cohen, Chair Mary Anne Royal Nancy Gause Kim Bery-Lee Kevin O'Kelly

L.D.1793, An Act to Improve Management and Reduce the Volume of Solid Waste
Testimony of: Melanie Loyzim/DEP Public Hearing: 4/28/2025 Page 2 of 3
management and food recovery. There are state laws and rules already in place to
support these goals.
L.D. 1793 creates responsibilities for the Department that are redundant with existing statutory requirements in Title 38, Chapters 13 and 24 to plan for and restrict
management of solid waste in Maine. LD 1793 would create a new Task Force to
review the Department's recommendations to the Legislature under Title 38, Chapter 24
for statewide waste management planning and Chapter 18 for Product Stewardship.
Quite frankly, it appears to relieve the Legislature of its current responsibility to consider the Departments recommendations under these existing laws by creating an
intermediary Task Force. The Department is currently required to submit annual recommendations for management of wastes through product stewardship programs, a biennial assessment of municipal solid waste management, and a 5-year update to the statewide plan for management of solid waste. LD 1793 appears to be based either in disagreement with the Departments recommendations presented through those
planning processes, or disappointment with the Legislature's utilization of those
recommendations to regulate waste management in Maine. LD 1793 would create a waste management planning process that is redundant, but would be scheduled to occur in a way that is out of sync with those other statutorily-required review and
planning processes.
LD 1793 also grants a broad authority to the Department that is very restrictive. When
issuing any new or amended license for a solid waste facility, it requires the Department to "take all action necessary to ensure" that wastes are managed in a manner consistent with multiple waste management hierarchies. This would apply not only to
landfill expansions, but also to municipal transfer stations that want to add a baler and to composting facilities proposing to change their inputs. lt creates a significant litigation
risk for licensees, as any licensing decision regarding management of solid waste in
Maine could be challenged and judged against this standard.

L.D.1793, An Act to improve Management and Reduce the Volume of Solid Waste
Testimony of: Melanie Loyzim/DEP Public Hearing: 4/28/2025 Page 3 of3
Sections 3 and 4 would apply to all persons with a solid waste license, including municipalities. All of the information provided to the Department in a license application
and in annual reports is a matter of public record available to anyone who requests it. lt is unclear what additional information is contemplated by LD 1793 that is not already
required as part of solid waste facility licenses and annual reports, or if the intention of
LD 1793 is to simply require that the Department make those annual reports readily
accessible to the public.
Section 6 of the bill would require the Department to implement a pilot program to
"evaluate innovative solid waste management solutions" and to report on this program to the Legislature in 2027. The Department currently utilizes the limited funding available in the Solid Waste Management Fund to support the legislatively proscribed Diversion Grants Program. it is unclear if LD 1793 intends to redirect this existing Other Special Revenue or anticipates that other funding would be provided to the Department
for this pilot program.
The Department recognizes that LD 1793 is likely born from disagreement with
recommendations and/or decisions by the Department under existing statutory
provisions for solid waste facility licensing. Rather than creating new statutory
provisions and additional planning exercises for the Department, the Department recommends that the Legislature identify whatever revisions to existing law are needed to achieve the desired, but un-obtained outcomes.
Thank you for the opportunity for this testimony and I would be happy to answer any questions you have now or at worksession.

Testimony of Senator Nicole Grohoski in support of
LD 1793, An Act to Improve Management and Reduce the Volume of Solid Waste
Before the Committee on Environment and Natural Resources April 28, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and distinguished members of the Committee on
Environment and Natural Resources, my name is Nicole Grohoski, and I represent Senate District 7, which covers most of Hancock County. I am pleased to present LD 1793, "An Act to
Improve Management and Reduce the Volume of Solid Waste."
Summary of the Bill
This bill is a comprehensive step forward in strengthening Maine's ability to manage waste in an environmentally and economically responsible way. Specifically it:
0 Clarifies the Department of Environmental Protecti0n's authority to ensure waste management practices align with Maine's priorities of waste reduction, recycling, and
pollution prevention.
0 Establishes a new Waste Solutions Task Force to bring municipalities, haulers, processors, and landfill operators together to identify cost-effective waste management
solutions.
O Requires applicants for new or amended solid waste facility licenses to engage meaningfully with surrounding communities and demonstrate how community input
infonns facility operations.
O Improves transparency by requiring annual public reporting on waste origins, volumes, and final destinations.
0 Expands eligibility for the Maine Solid Waste Diversion Grant Program to support a broader range of waste reduction activities.
O Creates a pilot program to test innovative, cost-saving waste management approaches, including regional cooperation and waste volume reduction strategies.

Why This Bill Is Needed

Maine's waste management challenges are mounting. Our state's solid waste diversion rate ---- the amount of material recycled, composted, or otherwise kept out of landfills ---- has plateaued
and, in some areas, declined. Without stronger Waste diversion programs, we are exhausting state
landfill capacity well ahead of schedule. Communities are paying ever-higher tipping fees, which are reflected in property tax increases, and the public is concerned about the environmental and health impacts of inadequate solid waste management.

Moreover, Maine's aging solid waste infrastructure and limited regional coordination often leave
municipalities on their own to solve these complex and expensive challenges. The failing solid
waste management "system" in my region is a top concern that municipal leaders ask me to take
action on. Nearly all municipal solid waste in eastem Maine is going straight to the Juniper
Ridge Landfill at this time. A few towns are recycling limited materials, and some private
residents and businesses are composting, but that's about it.

As outlined in Maine's Solid Waste Management Hierarchy, the most environmentally and
economically beneficial actions --- waste reduction, reuse, and recycling -- must be prioritized
above Iandfilling, which should only be a last resort.

This bill tackles the problem that municipalities face head-on by fostering collaboration, piloting

regional waste management models, and providing more robust support to towns and cities. It
enhances transparency ---- by making waste flow data available to the public -- to empower

municipalities, policymakers, and residents to make informed decisions and ensure that our

waste management system serves the public interest.

�

Maine has already laid important groundwork through its product stewardship programs
(including EPR for packaging), by encouraging composting, and supporting community initiatives like tool-lending libraries and repair caf�s. LD 1793 builds on these efforts by offering
municipalities more tools, greater transparency, and new pathways for collaboration.

Conclusion

This bill offers smart, forward-thinking strategies to modernize Maine's waste management
system. By fostering regional cooperation, strengthening public oversight, and elevating Waste reduction efforts, we can protect our environment, safeguard public health, and ensure that
taxpayer dollars are spent efficiently.
Thank you for your time and consideration of this legislation.

Testimony in Support of LD 1793,
An Act to Improve Management and Reduce the Volume of Solid Waste
Vanessa Berry, NRCM Sustainable Maine Program Manager
April 28, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Environment and Natural Resources, my name is Vanessa Beny. I am the Sustainable Maine
Program Manager for the Natural Resources Council of Maine (NRCM). I appreciate this
opportunity to testify in support of LD 1793.
Last year, the Maine Climate Council established a temporary Materials Management Task Force
(MMTF) to examine climate-related issues in solid waste management. This group brought
together a diverse range of stakeholders, including compost facility operators, wastewater treatment plant managers, large retailers, nonprofit organizations, and agency staff.
One of the most valuable outcomes of the MMTF was the creation of a network of partners
committed to solving Maine's solid waste challenges. In a "home rule" state with wide
demographic and geographic diversity, opportunities for such cross-sector collaboration are rare.
The MMTF provided a much-needed space for open dialogue and joint problem-solving among
stakeholders with a shared goal.
NRCM was fortunate to participate in those discussions, which covered complex topics such as
efficient hauling of materials, expanding recovery opportunities in rural areas, and reducing wasted food.
A consistent theme that emerged was the urgent need for regional partnerships. Stakeholders
recognized that investing in regional assets could lower operating costs for individual
communities and help towns work together to achieve economies of scale. Currently, rural and
less populated areas face significant barriers to accessing waste diversion altematives like recycling and composting. Regional collaboration offers a pathway to overcome cost and logistical
challenges and to establish infiastructure that would be unattainable for many towns on their own
LD 1793 proposes several critical steps to support more sustainable waste management practices
in Maine:
1. Create an Official Task Force for Materials Management - This would allow key
stakeholders to meet regularly to identify critical issues and propose policy solutions on a
biennial basis.
2. Promote Community Engagement - Facilities would be required to solicit and respond to community input during new or revised licensing processes.
3. Increase Transparency from Waste Facility Operators -- Licensed facilities would report annually on the origin, volume, and disposition of the waste they process.

4. Finance Regional Projects -~ Maine's Solid Waste Diversion Grant Program would be � expanded to fund regional collaboration projects between towns.
5. Implement a Pilot Program --~ The DEP would develop a pilot program to evaluate
innovative solid waste management solutions, including testing new diversion strategies
and cost-saving measures.
LD 1793 provides an opportunity for the Legislature to drive meaningful, structural changes to
Maine's waste management system. By encouraging greater collaboration among coimnunities,
facilities, and regional planning offices, this bill supports solutions identified by the MMTF and
will help advance resource recovery across the state -- not just in urban centers, but also in rural areas that can greatly benefit from investment and resource-sharing.
We recognize that budgets and staff capacity for state departments and municipalities are tight,
and assigning additional responsibilities to the Department of Environmental Protection at this
time may be challenging. However, we urge the Committee to consider many of the components of this bill and move forward with a proposal that fosters regional coordination, strengthens local
engagement, and promotes greater transparency within Maine's materials management sector.
Thank you for considering our comments. I would be happy to answer any questions for this
Committee now and in advance of the work session.
10046885:
Testimony in support of LD 1793 Act to Improve Management and Reduce the Volume of Solid Waste
Victor Horton, Executive Director Maine Resource Recovery Association (MRRA)
April 28, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Environment and Natural Resources.
I appreciate the opportunity to testify in support of LD 1793, which proposes to clarify the DEPs authority to manage waste, convene a task force to study that waste waste generated in Maine and among other things to specify through licensing ways in which that waste will be dealt with and hopefully to minimize how much waste is needed to be incinerated and and landfilled in the state of Maine.
This bill seems to clarify that a new license be given with regards to collaboration among neighboring communities.
Town and City solid waste budget line items are likely among the highest expenses. We all make waste in one form or another and it costs a lot to dispose of it. What a unique approach to offer grants and entertain plans for technology that is possibly in its infancy and could be very helpful in mitigating what we leave behind on this planet.
We commend the framers of the bill and hope for its success.
Land is a precious commodity and they are not making any more of it.
We are encouraged with what this proposed bill LD 1793 seeks to accomplish and urge the committee to give it an Ought to Pass vote.
Thank you for your consideration of our comments.
Respectfully submitted Victor Horton
